results.title: Do Grep and AST Agree on Which Functions Are Dead Code?
results.description: I wanted a quick dead-code pass over the Python files in my my-git-manager repo (server.py, reply_comments.py, publish_devto.py, git_commit.py, and three scripts under scripts/) and had two options sitting right there in the stdlib: a regex over the source text, or ast. I assumed one would obviously be better and ran both for real to see by how much. The regex version is the kind of thing you'd write in thirty seconds: import re def grep_heuristic(src): defs = re.findall(r'^def (\w+)\(', src, re.MULTILINE) flags = [] for name in defs: total_calls = len(re.findall(re.escape(name) + r'\(', src)) if total_calls - 1 <= 0: # minus the def line itself return defs, flags The AST version walks the real parse tree and checks every Name and Attribute node instead of grepping text: import ast def ast_heuristic(src, path): tree = ast.parse(src, filename=path) defs, called_names = [], set() for node in ast.walk(tree): if isinstance(node, (ast. FunctionDef, ast. AsyncFunctionDef)): if isinstance(node, ast. Name): if isinstance(node, ast. Attribute): return defs, [d for d in defs if d not in called_names] Across all seven files, here's what each one actually flagged: grep total flagged: 5 ast total flagged: 9 grep-only (ast missed): set() ast-only (grep missed): { ('scripts/list_all_published_titles.py', '__enter__'), ('scripts/list_all_published_titles.py', '__exit__'), ('publish_devto.py', '__init__'), ('server.py', 'create_article'), } agreed on both: { ('server.py', 'get_github_profile'), ('server.py', 'generate_commit_message'), ('server.py', 'list_articles'), ('server.py', 'get_article_stats'), ('server.py', 'get_repo_stats'), The dunder methods (__init__, __enter__, __exit__) are an easy miss to explain: Python calls them implicitly through the object protocol, never by writing their literal name at a call site, so neither heuristic should expect to see them "called" in source text. That's a known blind spot for both approaches, not a disagreement between them — grep happened not to flag them here only because of what's near them in the file, not because it understood anything about dunder semantics. The actual disagreement is create_article, and it's a real example of regex's biggest weakness: it can't tell a call from a mention. I checked where grep thought it saw a call: def create_article(title: str, body_markdown: str, ...) -> dict: ... # 90 lines later, inside another function's docstring: """ create_article(title="X", published=False) — the duplicate check is But both tools agree on calling all five of those server.py functions "dead," and both are wrong in the same way. get_github_profile, get_repo_stats, list_articles, get_article_stats, and generate_commit_message are MCP tools, registered with @mcp.tool() and invoked by an MCP client through the protocol — never by another line of Python in this file calling their name directly. Neither static heuristic can see that kind of call, because it isn't a call in the AST or in the text at all; it's a dispatch table built at runtime from string tool names coming over a transport, resolved by the FastMCP framework after the fact. A tool function in this codebase can have real, live callers every day and still read as 0-reference dead code to any analysis that only looks at the file it's defined in. Timing was the other thing I measured, since I had the numbers anyway: server.py (1141 lines): grep 2.17ms, ast 8.03ms (~3.7x) reply_comments.py (460 lines): grep 0.72ms, ast 2.78ms (~3.9x) AST parsing costs roughly 4x the regex pass across every file I measured, consistently enough that it's clearly the tree construction overhead, not noise. For a one-off check on a file this size that's still under 10 milliseconds — irrelevant in absolute terms, but it's not "free," and on a much larger codebase run frequently it's the kind of multiplier that does start to matter. So: for a quick first-pass sweep where occasional false negatives are tolerable, grep is three times cheaper and catches everything AST caught in my agreement set. For anything where the result actually drives a decision — deleting a function, flagging it in a PR review — the regex isn't just less precise, it's precise in a way you can't predict without rereading every result by hand, because you don't know whether a given hit is a real call or an English sentence that happens to look like one until you check. And for any codebase where some fraction of your "unused" functions are actually registered callbacks, RPC handlers, Flask routes, or MCP tools — invoked by name from outside the file, through a mechanism neither tool can trace — both approaches need a third check layered on top: an allowlist, a decorator-aware exclusion, or just accepting that "no in-file callers" and "dead code" are two different claims that happen to usually overlap and sometimes don't.

results.title: How to Run and Monitor Minecraft Servers on Your Own Hardware
results.description: The short answer: put MineOps on the Linux or macOS machine you already own, and it creates and monitors your Minecraft servers from one dashboard. You don't need new hardware or a separate hosting contract to get live status, alerts, and backups in one place. What MineOps actually does MineOps creates new servers on your own hardware, ready to join, with plugins and mods from Modrinth. It also gives you live status, Discord and Slack alerts, world backups, and new servers in a few clicks, on the Linux or Mac machines you already own. Everything you run shows up in a single dashboard, so you're not tabbing between consoles. Getting started on hardware you already have MineOps works with Minecraft servers on Linux or macOS machines. If you keep Crafty Controller in Docker, MineOps finds the servers it runs, so existing setups don't need to be rebuilt from scratch. Paper, Purpur, and Pufferfish get every MineOps feature. If you run a different server type, check what applies to your setup before you plan around it. How monitoring reaches the dashboard A small agent on each machine connects out to MineOps, so the agent needs no open ports. This matters for anyone behind a home router or a locked-down firewall: the monitoring side doesn't require you to expose a new service. One thing people get wrong here: players still need their own way to reach the Minecraft server. The agent's outbound connection is about monitoring, not about making the game reachable. Plan your player access separately, whether that's a public address, a tunnel, or a VPN. What the alerts cover MineOps alerts cover machines offline, crash loops, low memory or disk, TPS drops, and failed backups. Those are the failures that usually go unnoticed until players complain, so wiring them to Discord or Slack means you hear about trouble before your community does. Backups and player insight MineOps runs scheduled world backups with checksums. A checksum tells you the backup file matches what was written, which is the difference between having a backup and believing you have one. MineOps shows who played, for how long, and your quietest hour for maintenance. That last one is practical: schedule restarts and updates when nobody is online instead of guessing. Control without giving up the keys Start, stop, moderation, and console stay off until you allow them, and every command lands in the audit log. If you run a server with other admins, that means you can hand out access without handing out a blank cheque. Limits, plans, and what happens when you grow If you go over a plan limit on MineOps, nothing is deleted and nothing stops. That's worth knowing if you're sizing a plan for a community that spikes on weekends. The Free plan is $0 forever, with 2 Minecraft servers, 1 machine, 2 members, and 5 alert rules. Put simply, two Minecraft servers on one machine are free for good, which covers a lot of small communities and test setups. Above that: The Plus plan is $4 per month, with 10 Minecraft servers, 2 machines, 3 members, and 25 alert rules. The Network plan is $7 per month, with 40 Minecraft servers, 5 machines, 10 members, and 100 alert rules. The Business plan is $25 per month, with 200 Minecraft servers, 20 machines, 50 members, and 500 alert rules. On MineOps, a year costs the same as ten months, so annual billing is the cheaper way to commit. MineOps prices are in US dollars, before any sales tax. Everyone gets 14 days of Network, once, with no card needed. When the trial ends you keep everything on the free plan, and you can subscribe whenever you like. If you're unsure which tier fits, start on the trial, watch your alert volume and server count, then pick the plan that matches reality rather than the one that matches your hopes. Who this fits This setup suits people who already run Linux or macOS boxes and want monitoring and management without adding another layer of vendor lock-in. It's less useful if your servers live somewhere you can't run the agent, or if you need a host to manage the underlying hardware for you. In those cases, this isn't the tool for the job. If self-hosting monitoring for your Minecraft servers is the goal, you can read more at https://mineopsdash.com.

results.title: Eisenkot Handed Mandate to Form Israel Government, Netanyahu on Back Foot
results.description: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has handed former army chief Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the country’s next government, a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hopes of staying in office after the October 27 election. Eisenkot is to receive the mandate formally at a ceremony at the President’s Residence on Sunday, after which he will have 28 days to put together a government, with Herzog able to grant an extension of up to 14 days. The decision followed a round of consultations with parties in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot, who leads the Yashar party, was recommended by 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu. Herzog’s office announced the choice on Saturday night, November 7, after he met both men. Eisenkot’s tally came from several camps. His Yisrael Beiteinu party, Together, Yisrael Beiteinu and the Democrats, which hold 48 seats between them, were joined by the Arab-led Ra’am with eight and the Joint List with 11. The two Arab alliances won a record 19 seats between them in the election. Netanyahu’s side lost ground at the last stage. His right-wing bloc won 53 seats, but its recommendations fell to 46 when United Torah Judaism, with seven seats, chose not to back anyone. The ultra-Orthodox party stayed out over broken promises on military exemptions for religious students. A strong show of recommendations, however, does not guarantee a working government. Eisenkot’s own bloc is 13 seats short of a majority without the Arab parties, and their recommendations do not commit them to joining his government. Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and other opposition leaders have also ruled out working with Ra’am and the Joint List. The Joint List has said it could back an opposition government from outside, while Ra’am has shown openness to joining one. Herzog himself acknowledged the difficulty. He said Eisenkot had won a clear majority of recommendations, but that it remained uncertain whether he could form a government because the parties refused to cooperate with one another. If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can task someone else with the job. That could be Netanyahu or another lawmaker, and the stalemate could drag on in a country that has been sent back to the polls repeatedly in recent years.
